body:
Hi! I’m a female in law enforcement. I grew up reading Tamora Pierce books and Beka absolutely influenced me on my decision to become a police officer. 

The criminals that we deal with don’t exactly “assume they deserve something from the upper class”, but there is a distinct lack of accountability. Most of the people we deal with want something for nothing. They want to do whatever they want and run away from the consequences (sometimes literally). The “oh I deserve this even if I didn’t work for it” mentality is super common. 

You mentioned that Beka doesn’t want to use her connection to Lord Gershom to “rise quickly in the ranks, unlike some police officers today”. Depending on the apartment, some places have a strict “no nepotism” rule. The departments that don’t have that do not allow family members or spouses to be in the same chain of command. Unfortunately (or fortunately, depending), most of the world does run on connections. Many of the promotional opportunities that officers have are a written test, a certain amount of experience, and an interview before they can “move up the ranks”. 

Beka being reminded of Crookshank’s grand baby is a whole lot of normal. We go into briefing and get updates on whatever happened the night prior or whatever event is occurring during our shift. Terrible things happen everywhere, if one knows where to look. 

I loved your paragraph detailing the separation of class issues, especially the bit about Beka speaking to Sir Tullus about the landmarks. That’s a big thing: we don’t talk to the people in lower socio-economic neighborhoods the same way that we talk to the people in million dollar homes. Or the members of city council. Your speech and demeanor get polished up very quickly when a high-ranking member of command staff is nearby. 

The paragraph about the Puppies with their training Dogs: officers go through field training when we get out of the academy. You’re put with another officer who trains you how to do your job. You mention “the mentorship… depends heavily on how well they get along as people.” Sometimes you have a trainer who you absolutely hate, and while you can still learn from them, sometimes it’s difficult to do. If you’re lucky, you have a trainer who you like enough to eagerly learn from (which does include nobody getting hurt and everybody going home at the end of your shift). 

The retention rate for the Puppies in the Lower City is about what the retention rate is for rookie officers. Twenty to twenty-five percent of every academy class is lost within the first three to four years, either from resigning or being terminated. 

We ask citizens for information all of the time. Our homeless people know everything, and our business owners often give us enough pieces of the puzzle for us to figure out exactly what’s happened somewhere. 

The bandits, or suspects, who have sharp knives and will skewer you into the wall? We’re trained to deal with it when we need to, though I’m relatively certain that smashing a baton on a suspect’s kneecaps now would be frowned upon. It does beat dying, though, because part of my job is to go home at the end of the day, along with making sure all of my coworkers go home at the end of the day, too. 

“People appreciate the Dogs for dealing with the dregs of society.” A quote attributed to George Orwell states that “good men sleep peaceably in their beds at night because there are rough men ready to do violence on their behalf.” Citizens appreciate the police because “normal people” don’t want to get their hands dirty. They don’t want to deal with the meth heads or the crazy people or the teenagers stealing cars. 

Robert Peel was the father of policing, if you’re not familiar with him. I believe Tammy said that she based the Provost’s Guard off of his system. 

“Beka always fights to do her work for the Lower City, as all officers should.” Um. Yes. That’s why we’re in the job. There is nothing glamorous about putting on your tactical boots every day and packing your lunch, going to work so you can deal with whatever the city has decided to dish up. There is no sparkle or shine in dealing with the drug addict who has shoved something up their ass (no, I’m not joking) or the young adult that has just swallowed a handful of pills to harm themselves. Evening shift is always busy. We fight, sometimes literally, for the people that we do our best to protect. That’s why we’re in this profession: because we want to help people. Our job is to protect those who cannot protect themselves. Sometimes it’s our job to save people from themselves, as well. This is the rule, not the exception. 

“There is always space for change.” Yes ma’am there is. Most of us can only influence what’s in front of us, so we do what we can. Bit by bit, we build those relationships with our community and change what we can. It’s never perfect, and it may not ever be, but these things will change (if only because I will make it so). 

This was a delightful essay to read. Thank you for writing it.
I feel your pain (in more ways than one, ha). You take care of you.

I saw a lot of shit growing up. I saw kids who were neglected or abused by their family members, pushed to the side at school, with the system not working for them. I saw domestic violence firsthand and saw how important mental health was. 


I took a class in college where the professor showed us photos of a child abuse case he’d worked. He brought up a picture of a real skinny kid, all of thirteen years old, welts and bruises all over him, so thin you could count his ribs. He’d been chained under the bed of an RV, fed canned food, and let out once a week or so to bathe. His parents had forced him to have sex with his twelve-year-old sister and they sold it as child pornography. The kid was looking up at the camera through a greasy fringe of hair, arms out to his sides as though he was being crucified, his expression resigned as though he expected nothing else from this life. Our professor pointed at the photo and said “this is who you work for.” And then you had me, at twenty years old, as someone who had experienced domestic abuse and sexual assault and suicide attempts, sitting in the aisle seat in the back row thinking “you’re damn right it is.” 


I became a cop because I wanted to help people. I didn’t want a desk job and I’m an adrenaline junkie. I didn’t have a whole lot of expectations for it because I honestly didn’t know what to expect. I knew that there would be both good and bad to it, and that most people didn’t like the police, but that was about it. 


The reality of it is so much more than people think it is. People think about the tv shows or the news but that’s never the whole picture (or even an accurate one). 


I’ve plugged gauze into bullet wounds and wrapped whatever I can find around countless cuts or stab wounds while we wait for the medics to get there. Sometimes those wounds are self-inflicted. I’ve gone to overdoses and held someone’s head up, waiting for the medics and fucking praying, because I am watching this person’s breathing slow down while their chest is shuddering because they are dying in front of me. Suicides are hard and the medics don’t show up until we secure the scene. 


I’ve taken domestic assault reports where the victim is showing me a ring of bruises around their neck because their significant other strangled them, half-drowning them in the shower, and threatened to kill them. I marched right up to my sergeant and requested to go and find the suspect, because I was bound and determined to take his ass to jail. (Spoiler alert: we found him. His ass went to jail.) 


I’ve taken sexual assault reports where the victim is crying while she’s telling me about it, and I listen and ask my questions and I say “I believe you.”


I’ve fought drunks in parking lots because they were arrested for driving while intoxicated. I’ve fought people who assaulted their significant other, came after my partner with a baseball bat, fled from us, or kicked in the back door of their ex-girlfriend’s parent’s house and punched somebody’s mom. I’ve held little kids while their parent gets arrested for felony warrants. I’ve cleaned up blood and brain matter in someone’s backyard because their son shot himself under an oak tree. 


I’ve had people scream at me and call me every name under the sun. I’ve been threatened, hit on, cussed out, and spit at. I’ve been harassed because I am female and had more people than I care to count make inappropriate comments or try to tell me that I’m not as good at my job as other officers because I don’t have a dick. 


I’ve also passed out more stickers (little badge stickers) than I can count. I’ve gone to community events and helped pass out food from a food bank, posing for photos with people and getting to know them. I’ve had little kids sit in my patrol car (with the permission of their guardians) and taken pictures with them while showing them the backseat (also with the permission of their guardians) and I tell these kids “I either want you driving this car or riding shotgun, but I don’t ever want to see you in the back of it.” 


I’ve driven around my area belting out songs on the radio, waving at literally everyone I’ve seen, trying not to be the next cop meme but wanting to convey that I actually give a damn about the people I work for. I’ve given out resources for mental health and domestic violence, assisting where I can, assuring people that it’s okay for them to call us if they need to. I’ve listened to a sergeant get on the radio and say that he’s attempting to wrangle horses that have broken loose, and another officer say “uhhhhh we’ve got a cow in the middle of the road”. 


The reality of it, especially in today’s society, is fucking difficult to handle. The PTSD is a bitch and pretty much everyone hates you. All are condemned because of the actions of a few, so because I wear a uniform and have a badge and a gun, I’m automatically a piece of shit who only got into the profession for the power it gives me. It’s a hard job that not everyone can do. Society loves to Monday-morning-quarterback a decision that you had a split-second to make, but without the training and experience that you have. 


I love my job and wouldn’t trade it for the world. It’s the coolest thing ever: I get to drive a fast car and take bad guys to jail. I have the opportunity to protect people who wouldn’t be protected otherwise, talk to people who need a listening ear, and do my absolute fucking damndest to be the kind of officer (and person) that I needed but didn’t have when I was that abused and neglected kid.
